title: Prevention of arterial catheter-related bloodstream infections: current evidence and future directions
one_line_summary: Arterial catheters carry a bloodstream infection risk comparable to central lines, requiring dedicated prevention bundles across their lifecycle including chlorhexidine antisepsis, impregnated dressings, and proactive device stewardship.
key_pearls: The incidence density of arterial catheter-related bloodstream infections (**AC-CRBSI**) ranges from **0.1 to 0.4 per 1,000 catheter days**, approaching the infectious risk of central venous catheters (**CVCs**).

Cutaneous antisepsis with an **alcohol-based 2% chlorhexidine gluconate (CHG)** solution **significantly** reduces **CRBSI** risk compared to povidone-iodine during both catheter insertion and dressing changes.

Routine replacement of **transparent occlusive dressings** and **administration sets** every **7 days** is safe and non-**inferior** to more frequent changes unless dressings or tubing become disrupted or soiled.
Routine **scheduled catheter replacement** for arterial lines is **not supported** by current evidence and should only be performed when clinically indicated or upon device failure.
Real-time **ultrasound guidance** is **recommended** for radial and femoral arterial access (**GRADE 1**) to reduce mechanical complications and procedural time.
Blood cultures drawn from an indwelling arterial catheter demonstrate **non-inferior contamination rates** compared to peripheral venipuncture in **critically** ill patients.

sections.heading: Pathophysiology, Diagnosis, and Surveillance
sections.content:
- **Pathophysiology**: **AC-CRBSI** originates via extraluminal migration of skin flora along the external catheter surface (predominant early post-insertion) or intraluminal contamination of the catheter hub during routine manipulations.
- **Diagnostic criteria**: Confirmation requires matching microbiology between peripheral blood cultures and catheter-tip culture or differential time to positivity (**dTTP**).
- **Blood culture reliability**: Blood cultures drawn from **arterial catheters (ACs)** demonstrate non-**inferior** contamination rates compared to percutaneous venipuncture in **critically** ill patients; at least one set should be drawn from the **AC** when evaluating sepsis of unknown origin.
- **Surveillance limitations**: Traditional **CLABSI** surveillance metrics falsely attribute **AC-CRBSI** to co-existing **CVCs**; broader metrics like catheter-associated bloodstream infection (**CABSI**) and hospital-onset bacteremia (**HOB**) better capture total device infectious burden.
section_pearls: Blood culture contamination from arterial lines is non-inferior to peripheral venipuncture in ICU patients.
CLABSI surveillance underreports arterial catheter infections when central lines are concurrently present.

sections.heading: Catheter Stewardship and Site Selection
sections.content:
- **Catheter stewardship**: **ACs** should be inserted only for explicit clinical indications and removed immediately when no longer necessary; a deferred catheterisation strategy in shock patients is non-**inferior** regarding **28-day mortality**.
- **Femoral vs. radial site selection**: Post-hoc trial analyses show similar **CRBSI** risk between **femoral** and **radial** sites, although femoral catheters exhibit higher rates of catheter tip colonisation (**gram-negative bacilli**).
- **Anatomical position**: Radial **ACs** placed distally near the wrist joint may carry a higher risk of failure and **AC-CRBSI** compared to more proximal placement along the forearm.
section_pearls: Femoral and radial arterial catheters exhibit similar overall CRBSI rates despite higher colonisation at femoral sites.
Deferring arterial line insertion in shock patients until meeting specific safety criteria does not increase 28-day mortality.

sections.heading: Insertion Bundles: Barrier Precautions, Ultrasound, and Kits
sections.content:
- **Barrier precautions**: Evidence comparing maximal sterile barrier precautions (**MSBP**) to sterile barrier precautions (**SBP**) in radial lines remains inconclusive, though procedural asepsis as part of an insertion bundle successfully reduces extraluminal colonisation.
- **Ultrasound guidance**: Endorsed as a **GRADE 1** recommendation for radial and femoral cannulation to decrease mechanical complications, first-attempt failures, and procedural duration.
- **Standardised insertion packs**: Pre-assembled procedure kits enhance guideline adherence, lower phlebitis and device failure rates, and improve procedural efficiency.
- **Provider training**: Simulation-based procedural training focusing on aseptic technique under ultrasound guidance **significantly** improves clinician competency and reduces device-related infections.
section_pearls: Ultrasound guidance is a GRADE 1 recommendation for arterial catheterisation across radial and femoral sites.
Standardised insertion packs reduce procedural variation and improve adherence to aseptic bundles.

sections.heading: Antisepsis, Dressings, and Securement
sections.content:
- **Cutaneous antisepsis**: Skin preparation using **2% chlorhexidine gluconate (CHG) in 70% isopropyl alcohol** is **significantly** **superior** to povidone-iodine solutions for preventing **CRBSI** at insertion and during maintenance.
- **CHG-impregnated dressings**: **CHG-impregnated dressings** (gel pads or sponges) **significantly** reduce catheter colonisation and **CRBSI** compared to standard non-antimicrobial transparent dressings or gauze.
- **Dressing replacement intervals**: Scheduled replacement of intact, unsoiled transparent dressings every **7 days** is safe and non-**inferior** to shorter intervals (**3 days**); gauze dressings require replacement every **1 to 2 days**.
- **Catheter securement**: Sutureless securement devices (**SSD**) and traditional sutures display **equivalent** efficacy for **AC-CRBSI** prevention in existing clinical trial data.
section_pearls: 2% CHG in 70% isopropyl alcohol is the preferred cutaneous antiseptic for insertion and dressing changes.
Transparent dressings can be safely maintained for up to 7 days if clean, dry, and intact.

sections.heading: Maintenance, Access, and Replacement Strategies
sections.content:
- **Hub access and decontamination**: Strict hand hygiene, aseptic non-touch technique (**ANTT**), and access port scrubbing with **2% CHG-alcohol** before system entry are **critical** to prevent intraluminal hub contamination.
- **Administration sets**: Scheduled replacement of pressurised arterial fluid administration sets every **7 days** is non-**inferior** and safe compared to 3- to 4-day interval replacements.
- **Flush solution**: Continuous flush systems utilizing **0.9% normal saline** are standard; adding heparin may prolong line patency but does not alter infectious risk.
- **Scheduled catheter replacement**: Routine scheduled changing of indwelling **ACs** is **not recommended** and does not decrease **AC-CRBSI** rates compared to clinically indicated removal.
section_pearls: Administration sets for arterial lines can safely be changed at 7-day intervals.
Routine scheduled replacement of arterial lines to prevent infection is not supported by evidence.

strengths_limitations:
- **Strengths**: Comprehensive overview of the complete arterial catheter lifecycle; synthesizes findings from major RCTs, international guidelines, and novel surveillance metrics.
- **Limitations**: High-level evidence specific to arterial catheters remains scarce, forcing reliance on CVC extrapolations; **significant** heterogeneity exists across international guidelines regarding insertion bundles and surveillance definition.
